source.title: Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models
source.authors: Aidan Clark; D. de Las Casas; Aurelia Guy; Arthur Mensch; Michela Paganini; Jordan Hoffmann; Bogdan Damoc; Blake A. Hechtman; Trevor Cai; Sebastian Borgeaud; George van den Driessche; Eliza Rutherford; T. Hennigan; Matthew G. Johnson; Katie Millican; Albin Cassirer; Chris Jones; Elena Buchatskaya; D. Budden; L. Sifre; Simon Osindero; O. Vinyals; Jack W. Rae; Erich Elsen; K. Kavukcuoglu; K. Simonyan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures validation loss across routed-language-model sizes and expert counts, fits scaling laws, and evaluates their predictive fit. This tests scaling behavior with a different architecture and setup from the original dense-model studies.
record.gate_note: The study trains routed models at several base sizes and expert counts and reports validation-loss scaling fits and held-out fit errors. It also evaluates zero-shot transfer scaling. The main sweep uses 130B training tokens; it does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Values cited from other studies are not cataloged as results.
record.test_reason: The study fits power-law loss scaling for dense and routed (mixture-of-experts) transformer LMs. These span 15M–1.3B base sizes and 1–512 experts, all trained on 130B tokens. Its dense fit reproduces Kaplan's αN (0.078 vs 0.076). It shows how the fitted laws depend on functional form, base size, token count and schedule position, and it fits scaling on zero-shot transfer datasets. This applies the claim to a new model class, routed LMs, and reports results on V1, V4, V6 and V7. It does not test compute-optimal allocation or extrapolation to much larger runs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that routed LM validation loss follows a bilinear law in log base size and log expert count, with saturation in E. This law generalises Kaplan's dense law and holds across S-BASE, RL-R and HASH routing. Re-expressed in inference FLOPs and total parameters, it covers K and R variants. Gains from experts diminish with base size, and the implied cutoffs are about 937B (S-BASE) and about 85B (RL-R, HASH). An effective parameter count puts dense and routed models on one power law. They stress that all values are conditional on the 130B-token budget and schedule, that convergence is not reached, and that downstream scaling coefficients vary by task.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests routed Transformer architectures rather than the original dense-model scaling setup; it varies base size and expert count and fits joint laws for these variables and for inference FLOPs and parameter utilization. The main sweep holds training to 130B tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with fit form (separable, bilinear, or bounded); expert-count exponent varies with base size; scaling behavior varies with token count and learning-rate-schedule position; downstream coefficients differ by task and routing method; K and R alter the loss surface in N,E coordinates, with R=0.25 deviating slightly in F,B coordinates.

fits_no_version.finding: For routed LMs, the gain from adding experts follows a power law in E whose exponent shrinks with base size and saturates at high E. This implies routing stops helping beyond a cutoff size (937B for S-BASE, 85B for RL-R, 83B for HASH, at 130B tokens).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In mixture-of-experts LMs, loss improvement from expert count follows a bounded power law whose exponent diminishes with base model size.

record.problems: The main sweep uses a fixed 130B-token training amount and the authors acknowledge that models have not converged. They trained too many models to run multiple seeds for each; the seed check covers a 130M model at selected settings only. The claimed broad extrapolation is evaluated by leave-one-out fit errors within the tested sweep, and extreme N and E regimes are limited.
record.rows_left_out: None. The 60-row limit is reached; reported task-specific fit coefficients are included for all tasks and methods in Table 9.

untested.parts: Not tested. Leave-one-out RMSLE is within the 15M–1.3B sweep. The single 7B RL-R run used a different batch size and hyperparameters, and the authors say concrete extrapolation to it is impossible.
Not tested. There is no fixed-compute search over parameter and token counts; all main runs use 130B tokens.
Not tested. Only text pretraining; no other modalities, repeated data or fine-tuning.
Depth, width and aspect ratio at fixed parameter count are not varied. Only routing details K and R are.
Token-count power law not fitted: one token budget in the main sweep, plus three durations for 15M HASH models only. Compute scaling is not fitted for dense models.

missing.what: Dense size exponent a increases monotonically with training steps S, while power-law fits stay good at every S. Kaplan's L(N,S) form (Eq. 1.6) fails to fit their learning curves. This bears on V7 (schedule and token dependence) and on V1 (power-law fit quality across S).
All dense and routed models fall on a single power law in Effective Parameter Count across four orders of magnitude.
The a(E) table shows the base-size exponent changes with expert count (S-BASE 0.077 at E=4 to 0.060 at E=512). Table 7 gives the Eq. 7 fit coefficients.
A single 7B-base RL-R run (64 experts, different batch size and hyperparameters) still beats dense, but the authors say their laws cannot predict it because the setup changed.
Routing-frequency sweeps down to a single routed layer: S-BASE improves with frequency, HASH flattens, and R=1/L deviates.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. V2 labels were removed: leave-one-out error within the sweep is not extrapolation, and the authors say their own 7B run cannot be predicted. V4 bears only loosely, since K and R are routing details rather than depth or width. The 'zero-shot' tasks are fitted as transfer-set losses with power laws, not as accuracy, so V6 support concerns transfer loss. The reader's V7 label on the downstream rows (r37–r60) was dropped, because those rows were not linked to V7; task variation is labelled under V6 instead. Table 6 omits the 55M column, and its parenthesised values are hold-out RMSEs, not uncertainty on b. Tranche is T3 (new model class) rather than T2.

versions.untested_parts: The main sweep varies base model size and expert count, and the paper also fits loss against inference FLOPs and parameter utilization. It does not vary training tokens in the main sweep or establish independent parameter-, token-, and compute-scaling laws when other quantities are non-bottlenecks.
Prediction is assessed within the routed-model sweep using leave-one-out fit error; the study does not test extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger than all fitted runs.
No fixed-compute-budget search for loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
Tests routing frequency R and experts-per-datapoint K, not a broad range of depth, width, or other architecture details.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer-training regimes.
Reports zero-shot downstream-task scaling fits, but does not establish a general mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
Shows dependence on fit form, token count and training-schedule position, and downstream task. Does not test parameter-counting conventions or broadly compare datasets and training schedules.

rows.subject: Sinkhorn-BASE routed models
rows.operation_detail: Compare loss surfaces after changing experts per datapoint K; fit using inference FLOPs F and parameter utilization B
rows.measure: Validation loss scaling across architecture variants
rows.value: The shared fit across K values shows no substantial difference in performance
rows.note: Higher K gives better performance per step but is not necessarily more FLOP-efficient; K=1 is always on the Pareto front.
rows.check: K is a routing detail, not depth or width, so the link to V4 is loose. Equivalence holds only after re-parameterising by inference FLOPs F and parameter ratio B. In (N,E) coordinates the loss surfaces differ.

rows.subject: Sinkhorn-BASE routed models
rows.operation_detail: Compare loss surfaces after changing routed-layer frequency R; fit using inference FLOPs F and parameter utilization B
rows.measure: Validation loss scaling across architecture variants
rows.value: Loss surfaces in (F, B) are almost the same; R=0.25 deviates slightly
rows.note: The paper reports that architectural details K and R have little effect on scaling behavior, while noting this deviation.
rows.check: R=0.25 deviates slightly. Appendix D.2/D.4 show lower routing frequencies (down to a single routed layer) change performance, and HASH and S-BASE respond differently. These results are not captured in rows.

source_check.correct: state=observed for V4 in the stated R={0.25,0.5,1.0} comparison: nearly coincident loss surfaces with a slight deviation at R=0.25. Stronger departures at a single routed layer require a separate condition.
source_check.problem: V4 already permits slight architecture effects; the stated slight deviation does not establish partial rather than nearly full agreement.

relationships.condition: Dense models and per-base-size expert-count fits, at 130B tokens
relationships.reason: Dense αN=0.078 closely matches Kaplan's 0.076 (r13), and validation fits have low RMSE (r37, r43, r49, r55). Per-N power laws in E fit with leave-one-out RMSLE 19e-4 to 46e-4 (r10–r12).
relationships.display_finding: The dense parameter exponent was 0.078 versus the prior 0.076, validation fits had low RMSE, and expert-number power laws achieved leave-one-out RMSLE of 19×10^−4 to 46×10^−4.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Dense models and per-base-size expert-count fits, at 130B tokens
source_check.reason: Tables 1, 2 and 9 support power-law fits in the tested fixed-token setting: dense alpha_N=0.078 and per-base-size expert fits with RMSLE 19e-4 to 46e-4.

relationships.condition: Routed models, where total parameters grow via expert count
relationships.reason: Loss is not a single power law in parameters. The expert-count exponent shrinks with base size (-0.035 to -0.015, r17–r31), and scaling saturates at high E (Emax 314–478, r14–r16).
relationships.display_finding: The expert exponent shifted from −0.035 to −0.015 as base size increased, with saturation estimates of 314–478 experts.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Routed models, where total parameters grow via expert count
source_check.reason: Sections 4.2–4.3 and Tables 3 and 6 show size-dependent expert slopes and clear saturation, qualifying a single power law in raw parameter count.

relationships.condition: Functional form, base size and bounded expert scaling
relationships.reason: Joint fit error depends on form: separable 80–90e-4 vs bounded 56–58e-4 (r1–r9). The exponent b varies with N (r17–r31). The best fit needs a saturating transform in E (r14–r16).
relationships.display_finding: A bounded form reduces joint fit error from (80–90)×10⁻⁴ to (56–58)×10⁻⁴, while exponent b varies with base size and the best fit requires saturation with expert number.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Functional form, base size and bounded expert scaling
source_check.reason: Table 1 shows fit errors changing with functional form; Table 6 shows expert slopes changing with base size; Section 4.3 documents curvature requiring bounded expert scaling.

relationships.condition: Token count and learning-rate schedule position (15M HASH runs)
relationships.reason: Models are unconverged at 130B tokens (r34, r35). The expert exponent b depends on token count and on position in the cosine schedule, not on token count alone (r36).
relationships.display_finding: The 15M HASH models remain unconverged at 130B tokens, and expert exponent b depends on both token exposure and position in the cosine schedule.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Token count and learning-rate schedule position (15M HASH runs)
source_check.reason: Appendix F.1–F.2 reports continued improvement beyond 130B tokens and expert slopes depending on both token count and position within the learning-rate schedule.

relationships.condition: Experts per datapoint K∈{1,2,4}, after re-parameterising by inference FLOPs and total parameters
relationships.reason: Joint fits across K show no substantial difference in the (F,B) coordinates (r32).
relationships.display_finding: Joint fits for 1, 2 and 4 experts per datapoint showed no substantial differences after accounting for inference FLOPs and total parameters.

relationships.condition: Routing frequency R, especially R=0.25 and lower
relationships.reason: Loss surfaces are almost the same for R∈{0.5,1.0}, but R=0.25 deviates slightly (r33). The text shows larger deviations at a single routed layer, not captured in rows.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Routing frequency R, especially R=0.25 and lower
source_check.reason: Appendix D.4 supports qualification for very sparse routing, especially a single routed layer. The slight R=0.25 deviation alone remains compatible with V4 and does not justify a partial state for r33.
